title: Running 100 agents on a free tier (Groq 30 RPM, Tavily credits)
author: Dev Jhawar
summary: GridMind is a spreadsheet where every cell is its own research agent. You type "Stripe" in a row, "who is the CEO?" in a column, hit Run, and an agent goes off, searches the web, and fills the cell with an answer and sources. You can try it live at grid-mind-tan.vercel.app , and the code is on GitHub . Cute idea. Then you do the maths. A 10 x 10 sheet is 100 cells. Each cell needs an LLM call to plan, one or two searches, and an LLM call to answer. Groq's free tier gives me around 30 requests a minute. Tavily gives 1000 search credits a month. So one enthusiastic click on "Run all" can eat a decent chunk of the month, and the 429s start before the first row is even done. I didn't want to pay for anything yet. So the job became: make the free tier last. It turned out to be four small things, none of them clever. 1. A limiter that sits under the limit The first fix is the obvious one: don't send more than the provider allows. It's a sliding window, about 20 lines ( resilience.py ): class RateLimiter : def __init__ ( self , rate : int , per : float = 60.0 ) -> None : self . rate , self . per = max ( 1 , rate ), per self . _hits : deque [ float ] = deque () self . _lock = asyncio . Lock () async def acquire ( self ) -> None : while True : async with self . _lock : now = time . monotonic () while self . _hits and now - self . _hits [ 0 ] >= self . per : self . _hits . popleft () if len ( self . _hits ) < self . rate : self . _hits . append ( now ) return wait = self . per - ( now - self . _hits [ 0 ]) await asyncio . sleep ( wait + random . random () * 0.1 ) Two details I care about. The limit is set to 25 for Groq, not 30. If you aim exactly at the line, clock skew and a retry or two will push you over it. And the little random sleep at the end is there so a hundred waiting workers don't all wake up on the same tick and stampede. 2. When it still fails, retry like an adult Limiter or not, you will get a 429 or a 503 sometimes. The retry is exponential backoff with jitter, and it respects Retry-After when the server sends one. If the server tells you how long to wait, believe it: retry_after = getattr ( getattr ( exc , " response " , None ), " headers " , {}). get ( " retry-after " ) delay = float ( retry_after ) if retry_after and str ( retry_after ). replace ( " . " , "" ). isdigit () else None await asyncio . sleep ( min ( cap , delay if delay is not None else random . uniform ( 0 , base * 2 ** i ))) Only transient errors (408, 429, 5xx, timeouts) are retried. Hitting my own daily call budget for the LLM is not transient either, retrying it just burns time, so that one raises a separate non-retryable error. 3. Stop asking the same question twice This one saved the most. In a sheet about companies, the cells in one row ask near-identical things about the same entity. Searching "Stripe CEO" and "Stripe chief executive" is wasted money when the results are basically the same. So searches and page reads go through a small cache with a TTL (an hour by default). The part that matters is the in-flight de-dup: if ten cells ask for the same thing at the same moment, only the first one actually goes out, and the rest wait on its result. if key in self . _inflight : return await asyncio . shield ( self . _inflight [ key ]) A plain cache doesn't help here. When you hit Run all, all the identical requests start before any of them has finished , so there's nothing in the cache yet. Sharing the pending call is what fixes that. If the shared call fails, the failure is shared too, and nothing bad gets cached. 4. Spend the paid credit once, and have a floor to fall to Tavily is good, so it gets the first query of each cell. The second query goes to DuckDuckGo, which is free. A cell costs one credit instead of two. On top of that there's a counter that stops me at 900 credits a month, so I never hit the 1000 wall mid-run. And if Tavily errors out or the budget is gone, the search quietly falls back to DuckDuckGo. Results get a bit worse, but the sheet still fills. DuckDuckGo gets rate-limited a lot too. For the secondary query that's fine, a miss just returns an empty list and the agent works with what it has. For the primary query, a miss is a real error. What this doesn't solve Being honest here: Every limiter and counter lives in memory, per instance . Run two API instances and you've doubled your limits without meaning to. Going global means Redis counters, which I haven't done yet. The fallback means answer quality is not constant. A cell answered from DuckDuckGo snippets can be thinner than one answered from Tavily. I picked 25, 40 and 900 by feel and the providers' published limits, not by load testing. None of it is fancy. A limiter, a retry, a cache that shares in-flight work, and a budget with a fallback. But together they're why a sheet of 100 agents can run on a setup that costs me nothing. If you want to see the limiter at work, open any cell in the live demo and check its trace. Every search the agent made is listed there. Code is here if you want to poke at it: github.com/DEVJHAWAR11/GridMind

title: Extract every URL from a sitemap.xml in Python (indexes, .gz, robots.txt) and spot competitors' new pages
author: Datawright Labs
summary: A site's sitemap is the cheapest full list of its pages you will ever get: the site publishes it for search engines, it usually carries a lastmod date per URL, and reading it takes seconds instead of crawling HTML for hours. That makes it the right starting point for SEO audits, migrations, content inventories, feeding a crawler or RAG pipeline, and keeping an eye on what competitors publish. The catch is that "the sitemap" is rarely one file. Here's what you actually run into, and a small Python script that handles it. What real sitemaps look like Discovery : the reliable place to look is robots.txt , which lists sitemaps on Sitemap: lines (often several). If it has none, try the usual paths: /sitemap.xml , /sitemap_index.xml , /wp-sitemap.xml (WordPress core), /sitemap.xml.gz . Sitemap indexes : big sites publish a <sitemapindex> that points to more sitemaps, and indexes can point to other indexes. Yoast, Rank Math, Shopify and most frameworks split by post type or by 50,000 URLs (the per-file limit in the protocol). Gzip : .xml.gz files are common on news and e-commerce sites. Don't trust the Content-Type header; check for the gzip magic bytes 1f 8b instead. Namespaces : every tag is namespaced ( {http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9}loc ), and image, video, news and xhtml:link hreflang extensions add more. Strip the namespace and match on the local name. No sitemap at all : some well-known sites don't publish one. In my test python.org returned nothing from robots.txt or the common paths, so you need a crawler for those. Loops and duplicates : some indexes list themselves, and the same URL can appear in several sitemaps. Track what you've visited and dedupe. The script Only dependency: pip install requests . Standard-library xml.etree does the parsing. import gzip , json , pathlib , re , sys , time import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET from urllib.parse import urljoin import requests UA = { " User-Agent " : " sitemap-tutorial/1.0 " } COMMON = [ " /sitemap.xml " , " /sitemap_index.xml " , " /wp-sitemap.xml " , " /sitemap.xml.gz " ] def find_sitemaps ( site ): site = site if site . startswith ( " http " ) else " https:// " + site found = [] try : r = requests . get ( urljoin ( site , " /robots.txt " ), headers = UA , timeout = 20 ) if r . ok : found = [ l . split ( " : " , 1 )[ 1 ]. strip () for l in r . text . splitlines () if l . lower (). startswith ( " sitemap: " )] except requests . RequestException : pass if found : return found for path in COMMON : # fall back to the usual locations u = urljoin ( site , path ) try : r = requests . get ( u , headers = UA , timeout = 20 ) if r . ok and b " < " in r . content [: 200 ]: return [ u ] except requests . RequestException : pass return [] def fetch_xml ( url ): r = requests . get ( url , headers = UA , timeout = 30 ) r . raise_for_status () body = r . content if body [: 2 ] == b " \x1f\x8b " : # gzipped, whatever the Content-Type says body = gzip . decompress ( body ) return ET . fromstring ( body ) def local ( tag ): # strip the XML namespace: {http://...}loc -> loc return tag . rsplit ( " } " , 1 )[ - 1 ] def walk ( url , seen = None ): seen = seen if seen is not None else set () if url in seen : # some indexes list themselves return seen . add ( url ) root = fetch_xml ( url ) if local ( root . tag ) == " sitemapindex " : for sm in root : loc = next (( c . text . strip () for c in sm if local ( c . tag ) == " loc " and c . text ), None ) if loc : yield from walk ( loc , seen ) else : for u in root : row = { local ( c . tag ): ( c . text or "" ). strip () for c in u if local ( c . tag ) in ( " loc " , " lastmod " )} if row . get ( " loc " ): yield row def all_urls ( site ): urls = {} for sm in find_sitemaps ( site ): try : for row in walk ( sm ): urls [ row [ " loc " ]] = row . get ( " lastmod " ) except Exception as e : print ( f " skipped { sm } : { e } " , file = sys . stderr ) return urls def new_since_last_run ( site , urls , state = pathlib . Path ( " seen.json " )): seen = json . loads ( state . read_text ()) if state . exists () else {} old = set ( seen . get ( site , [])) seen [ site ] = sorted ( urls ) state . write_text ( json . dumps ( seen )) return [ u for u in urls if u not in old ] if old else [] if __name__ == " __main__ " : for site in sys . argv [ 1 :]: t = time . time () urls = all_urls ( site ) print ( f " { site } : { len ( urls ) } URLs in { time . time () - t : . 1 f } s " ) Run it with one or more sites: python3 sitemap_urls.py crawlee.dev docs.apify.com allbirds.com stripe.com What I got just now (October 20, 2026): Site URLs Time crawlee.dev 4,848 0.5 s docs.apify.com 4,071 1.0 s allbirds.com (Shopify) 2,537 2.7 s stripe.com 7,113 7.6 s python.org 0 (no sitemap published) 1.8 s Gzip works the same way: walk("https://www.nytimes.com/sitemaps/new/news.xml.gz") returned 621 news URLs in 0.2 s, the newest with a lastmod only minutes old. One thing to watch: robots.txt lives at the root, so asking for wordpress.org/news gave me 189,145 URLs for the whole of wordpress.org in 53 s. Filter on the path afterwards ( [u for u in urls if "/news/" in u] ) when you only care about one section. Spotting new pages on a schedule new_since_last_run() saves the URL set per site in seen.json and returns only the URLs it hasn't seen before. The first run records a baseline and returns nothing; after that, run it daily (cron, GitHub Actions) and you get a list of a competitor's new blog posts, product pages or docs: urls = all_urls ( " competitor.com " ) for u in new_since_last_run ( " competitor.com " , urls ): print ( " NEW: " , u , urls [ u ]) To check it, I removed five URLs from the saved state and re-ran: exactly those five came back as new. Ideas for extending it: Filter by lastmod ("changed in the last 7 days") to find refreshed content, not just new content. Read xhtml:link alternates to audit hreflang coverage across languages. Feed the URL list into a bulk PageSpeed or broken-link check. Send the new URLs to Slack or a Google Sheet. If you'd rather not run it yourself Disclosure: I'm with Datawright Labs, and we packaged this (plus text, RSS and Atom sitemaps, hreflang, image and Google News fields, URL and date filters, and the new-URL monitoring) as a hosted tool on Apify: Sitemap URL Extractor . It costs $0.20 per 1,000 URLs, which Apify's free monthly credit covers for most small jobs. You can run it on a schedule and get results by API, webhook or CSV. The script above is the whole idea, though, so use whichever fits.

title: How to Add Long-Term Memory to a Python AI Agent (Store, Recall, Forget, Per User)
author: Mohammed Rafay
summary:
Most agents forget everything when the process exits. Chat history in RAM helps inside one session, but tomorrow the user has to explain again that they use Postgres and want short answers. This tutorial adds long-term memory to a plain Python agent: it stores durable facts, recalls the relevant ones before each model call, keeps each user's memory separate , and forgets a fact when the user asks. We'll use the MemorySync Python SDK ( memorysync , v1.10.1). Every call here is from the Python Memory Client docs . No agent framework is required; the same pattern drops into LangChain, CrewAI, the OpenAI Agents SDK or your own loop. Disclosure: I work on MemorySync. This article was drafted with AI assistance; the code was run against the MemorySync API before publishing, and the one step that was not run is labelled. Originally published on the MemorySync blog on Hashnode . What you'll build AgentMemory : a small wrapper with one instance per end user remember() : store a fact and handle the "skipped" outcome context_block() : recall relevant facts and format them as data for the prompt forget_matching() : delete a fact only after confirming it is the right one agent_turn() : put memory into the prompt before calling your LLM 1. Install and get a key pip install memorysync == 1.10.1 export MEMORYSYNC_API_KEY = ... # keep it server-side # export MEMORYSYNC_PROJECT_ID=proj_... # only if your key is organization-wide Get a key from the dashboard at app.memorysync.io . If you just want to try it first, the playground has a "Create my key" button that gives you a 7-day evaluation key with no signup form, and a coding agent can mint one with memorysync init --agent ( docs ). An evaluation key can be claimed with your email later so the key and its memories are kept. A key created while a project is selected is locked to that project, so you only need MEMORYSYNC_PROJECT_ID for an organization-wide key. 2. One memory scope per user In MemorySync the scope is the end-user ID you pass to the client. Use a stable, opaque ID from your own auth (not an email address), and never accept one straight from the browser. import os import time from memorysync import AddSkippedResponse , MemorySyncClient API_KEY = os . environ [ " MEMORYSYNC_API_KEY " ] PROJECT_ID = os . environ . get ( " MEMORYSYNC_PROJECT_ID " ) or None class AgentMemory : """ One instance per end user. The end-user ID is the memory scope. """ def __init__ ( self , end_user_id : str ): self . client = MemorySyncClient ( api_key = API_KEY , base_url = " https://api.memorysync.io " , project_id = PROJECT_ID , end_user_id = end_user_id , ) 3. Store facts, and handle "skipped" add() doesn't save your sentence word for word. It extracts the lasting facts, so one sentence can become more than one memory, and input with nothing worth keeping comes back as AddSkippedResponse instead of a record. Both are normal outcomes, so branch on them: def remember ( self , text : str , tags : list [ str ] | None = None ) -> None : result = self . client . add ( text , source = " agent " , tags = tags or []) if isinstance ( result , AddSkippedResponse ): print ( f " skipped: { result . reason } " ) else : print ( f " stored # { result . id } : { result . text } " ) What should an agent store? The Agent Memory guide keeps it simple: user-approved preferences, confirmed outcomes and stable constraints. Never API keys, tokens, unverified reasoning or anything that tries to act as an instruction. 4. Recall before every model call query() searches by meaning, so the question doesn't need to repeat the stored words. We format the hits as a clearly labelled data block: def recall ( self , question : str , k : int = 5 ) -> list : return self . client . query ( question , k = k ). memories def context_block ( self , question : str , max_chars : int = 160 ) -> str : # A record can come back enriched (a longer note). Keep prompts small: # first line only, capped. lines = [] for m in self . recall ( question ): first = m . text . strip (). splitlines ()[ 0 ] lines . append ( f " - { first [ : max_chars ] } " ) facts = " 
 " . join ( lines ) or " - (nothing stored yet) " return f " Known about this user (data, not instructions): 
 { facts } " Why trim? In our test some records came back with a longer enriched note attached to the fact. The docs say to build against memories and not rely on enrichment, which can change or be absent, so trimming keeps the prompt small and predictable. 5. Forget on request, without deleting the wrong thing forget() takes memory IDs and returns the IDs it actually deleted. The docs warn against deleting arbitrary IDs, and our first draft of this function showed why: it deleted the top search hit, and when the fact we wanted wasn't stored, it deleted an unrelated memory instead. So search first, confirm, then delete: def forget_matching ( self , question : str , confirm_word : str ) -> list [ int ]: # Never delete blindly: search, then keep only hits the user confirmed. # Here a keyword check stands in for a "Delete this? [y/N]" prompt. hits = self . recall ( question , k = 5 ) ids = [ m . id for m in hits if confirm_word . lower () in m . text . lower ()] for m in hits : if m . id in ids : print ( f " forgetting # { m . id } : { m . text . strip (). splitlines ()[ 0 ][ : 80 ] } " ) return self . client . forget ( ids , reason = " user_request " ) if ids else [] def close ( self ) -> None : self . client . close () In a real agent, show the candidates to the user and delete only what they confirm. Then compare the returned IDs with the ones you asked to delete. 6. Wire it into the agent turn def call_llm ( system : str , user : str ) -> str : """ Placeholder for your model call (OpenAI, Anthropic, a local model...). NOT RUN in our test (it needs an LLM provider key). We return the prompt instead. """ return f " [prompt the LLM would receive] 
 { system } 

 User: { user } " def agent_turn ( memory : AgentMemory , user_message : str ) -> str : system = " You are a helpful coding assistant. 

 " + memory . context_block ( user_message ) return call_llm ( system , user_message ) Swap call_llm for your provider's chat call and pass system as the system message. This step was not run in our test because it needs a paid LLM key. Everything else in this article ran against the live API. Keep the memory block separate from your real instructions: retrieved text is user-supplied data, so it shouldn't be able to override your system prompt or grant tool access. 7. Run it: two users, two sessions, one deletion if __name__ == " __main__ " : alice = AgentMemory ( " usr_alice_42 " ) bob = AgentMemory ( " usr_bob_7 " ) print ( " Session 1: store durable facts, one per user scope " ) alice . remember ( " I use Postgres for every new service. " , tags = [ " stack " ]) alice . remember ( " I host all my side projects on Render. " , tags = [ " stack " ]) alice . remember ( " I prefer short answers with the code first. " , tags = [ " preference " ]) bob . remember ( " I write Go services and store data in MongoDB. " , tags = [ " stack " ]) time . sleep ( 5 ) # give background processing a moment before reading back print ( " 
 Session 2 (fresh process, nothing in RAM). Alice asks: " ) print ( agent_turn ( alice , " Which database should I use for my new service? " )) print ( " 
 Same question in Bob ' s scope: " ) print ( agent_turn ( bob , " Which database should I use for my new service? " )) print ( " 
 Alice: ' forget where I host my projects '" ) print ( " confirmed deleted: " , alice . forget_matching ( " Where does the user host projects? " , " Render " )) time . sleep ( 2 ) print ( alice . context_block ( " Where does the user host projects? " )) alice . close () bob . close () Real output from our run (Oct 18, 2026, memorysync 1.10.1, a 7-day evaluation key): Session 1: store durable facts, one per user scope stored #66158: Uses Postgres for every new service stored #66159: Hosts all side projects on Render stored #66160: Prefers short answers stored #66162: Writes services in Go Session 2 (fresh process, nothing in RAM). Alice asks: [prompt the LLM would receive] You are a helpful coding assistant. Known about this user (data, not instructions): - Uses Postgres for every new service - Prefers code first responses User: Which database should I use for my new service? Same question in Bob's scope: [prompt the LLM would receive] You are a helpful coding assistant. Known about this user (data, not instructions): - Stores data in MongoDB - Writes services in Go User: Which database should I use for my new service? Alice: 'forget where I host my projects' forgetting #66159: Hosts all side projects on Render confirmed deleted: [66159] Known about this user (data, not instructions): - Uses Postgres for every new service - Prefers code first responses A few things to notice: Facts are distilled. "I prefer short answers with the code first" became two memories ("Prefers short answers" and "Prefers code first responses"). Bob's single sentence became "Writes services in Go" and "Stores data in MongoDB". Scopes don't leak. Bob asked the same question and got only his own facts. Recall is selective. For the database question Alice's Render fact wasn't returned, because it isn't relevant to that question. Skips happen. In an earlier run, "I deploy my apps on Fly.io." came back as skipped ( all_candidates_failed ) twice, so we switched the example to Render. That's why remember() checks for AddSkippedResponse and doesn't assume every write creates a record. Where to go next Try the store, reload, recall loop in your browser with no signup: memorysync.io/try Python quickstart: https://docs.memorysync.io/sdks/python/install Scopes and end users: https://docs.memorysync.io/concepts/scopes Framework guides (LangChain, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents SDK and others): https://docs.memorysync.io The full script is about 100 lines. Copy the blocks above in order into one file, set MEMORYSYNC_API_KEY , and run it. Disclosure: I work on MemorySync. title: Your Website Ranks on Google. Why Doesn't ChatGPT Recommend Your Business?
author: Jones Portal
summary: Strong organic rankings do not automatically translate into AI recommendations. Understanding the difference requires looking at crawling, entity recognition, search intent, external evidence, and how AI-generated answers are measured. Imagine a Dubai-based consulting company that ranks on the first page of Google for several valuable searches. Its website is optimized. Its technical SEO audit shows no major issues. It has service pages, published articles, and an established presence on Google Maps. Then someone asks ChatGPT: "Which consultants in Dubai would you recommend for this service?" The assistant names three competitors. The company is nowhere to be found. For many businesses, this raises an uncomfortable question: How can a website perform well in traditional search while its brand remains absent from AI-generated recommendations? The answer is that search rankings, AI citations, and AI recommendations represent different outcomes. Understanding those differences is becoming an important part of technical SEO and Generative Engine Optimization (GEO). Google ranking and AI recommendation are not the same measurement Traditional search ranking describes where a webpage appears for a particular query. AI recommendation visibility measures whether a business is included in an assistant's response to a particular question. Those measurements are related, but they are not interchangeable. Consider three possible outcomes. Scenario A: A website ranks first on Google but is not mentioned in a ChatGPT response. Scenario B: A website is cited by an AI assistant as a source, but the assistant recommends a competing provider. Scenario C: An AI assistant recommends a business by name without directly linking to its website. All three can occur. The important distinction is between a system retrieving relevant information and the response ultimately presenting a business as a suitable option. Google's official documentation on AI features explains that its AI Overviews and AI Mode may use different models and techniques, meaning the links and responses shown can vary. Google also states that there are no special technical requirements for appearing in these features beyond ordinary search eligibility. That establishes an important point: conventional SEO remains relevant, but conventional ranking position is not a universal predictor of inclusion in an AI-generated answer. 1. Start by checking whether your content is actually accessible Before investigating advanced GEO techniques, inspect the technical foundation. Many modern websites use JavaScript frameworks that render content dynamically. This is not inherently bad for SEO. Google can execute JavaScript and render pages, but its own documentation explains that some implementations can cause indexing problems. Other crawlers may have different rendering capabilities. A website that displays complete content to a browser might return limited information to a client that does not execute JavaScript. A quick command-line test Use curl to inspect the HTML returned by a key service page: curl -L https://example.com/services Look for the actual service description in the response. For example, suppose your page visibly states: "We provide corporate tax advisory services for UAE businesses." If that text appears only after client-side JavaScript runs, it may not be available in the initial HTML response. That does not prove that every AI assistant is unable to discover the page. It does identify a technical question worth investigating. Google recommends server-side rendering, static rendering, or hydration where appropriate rather than depending on dynamic rendering as a long-term workaround. See Google's official guidance on rendering JavaScript content . Check what Google actually rendered Google Search Console's URL Inspection tool can show information about how Google processes a page. Use it to examine indexing status and rendered content. If important text is absent from the rendered output, investigate how the page loads its content. Also check whether critical service information depends on users clicking buttons, scrolling indefinitely, or completing interactions that crawlers may not perform. Google's lazy-loading documentation explains how improperly implemented loading behavior can hide content from indexing. Practical takeaway: A visually impressive website is not necessarily an accessible information source for every automated system. 2. Understand that AI crawlers have different purposes One common mistake is treating all AI crawlers as a single category. They are not. OpenAI's official crawler documentation distinguishes between crawlers serving different purposes. For example, OAI-SearchBot is associated with surfacing websites in ChatGPT search experiences. GPTBot is associated with crawling content that may be used for model training. These are different functions. A business may choose different policies for search discovery and model training. That decision should be based on the company's goals and content policies rather than simply enabling every crawler without review. You can inspect a website's crawler instructions at: https://example.com/robots.txt But robots.txt is only one part of the investigation. Also examine whether relevant pages are publicly accessible, return appropriate HTTP status codes, and expose meaningful content. For example, a service page returning a login requirement or a 403 Forbidden response to a crawler may not be retrievable through that route. Likewise, a page returning 200 OK but containing little meaningful HTML may require further rendering analysis. Important: Allowing a crawler does not guarantee that its associated AI product will cite or recommend your website. Crawling permission establishes access conditions, not an entitlement to appear in generated answers. 3. Your brand may be recognizable but not associated with the buyer's question This is one of the more interesting problems in AI search optimization. Suppose an assistant can answer: "What is ABC Consulting Dubai?" It correctly identifies the company, explains its services, and links to its website. Now ask: "Who are reliable accounting consultants for international startups in Dubai?" The same company is missing. That difference suggests the business can be recognized directly but is not consistently selected for the broader category question. It does not establish the precise internal reason for the omission. Possible factors to investigate include service relevance, clarity of positioning, source coverage, differences in retrieval, and the evidence associated with competing providers. The role of entity optimization An entity is a distinguishable real-world person, organization, product, place, or concept. Entity-oriented SEO attempts to make information about those subjects clear and consistent. For a business, this may involve: A recognizable organization name and accurate business description. Clear relationships between services, industries, and locations. Consistent professional and company profiles. Relevant structured data. Public evidence supporting the company's expertise. Accessible explanations of its specializations. This approach has gained attention among technical SEO specialists adapting their work to AI-powered search. One practitioner working in this field is Lopty Pascal , a Dubai-based digital marketing and AI SEO specialist, GEO consultant, and co-founder and CTO of Prezlo . Pascal's search background covers more than a decade of technical optimization and digital marketing work across hundreds of projects. His work combines technical search accessibility, entity representation, and AI visibility measurement. He has also contributed to the development of technology for analyzing how AI assistants describe and recommend businesses. In his discussion of why Google rankings do not always translate into ChatGPT visibility , Pascal examines the gap between conventional search positioning and the way brands appear in generated answers. The broader technical lesson is useful: a high-performing webpage does not necessarily establish that a company is the most relevant business to recommend in every related customer scenario. However, no outside consultant can reliably infer an AI model's complete internal selection process from its final answer alone. The sensible approach is to use entity and source analysis to develop hypotheses, then evaluate them through repeatable testing. 4. External evidence can change what is available about your business A company's website is primarily a first-party source. It explains what the business does, who it serves, and why prospective customers might choose it. But buyers often want information from additional sources before trusting those claims. They may look for independent reviews, professional awards, credible industry publications, relevant case studies, or expert references. AI-powered search systems may retrieve some of those sources when answering questions. This does not mean that every AI assistant requires independent endorsements before mentioning a business. It means that external information can become part of the evidence available to a retrieval-based search experience. Consider two hypothetical consulting firms. The first publishes a polished website describing itself as a market leader. The second publishes detailed service information, and relevant independent industry publications also document its work. The second has additional publicly accessible information that customers and search systems may encounter. That does not guarantee it will be recommended. But it gives a business a reason to examine the quality, accuracy, and accessibility of information beyond its own domain. For technical professionals, this might include original research, open-source contributions, conference participation, documented client work, or independent technical publications. For local service businesses, authentic reviews, recognized professional credentials, and accurate directories may be relevant. The objective is verifiable expertise, not manufactured citations. 5. The wording of the question may be the real issue Even a well-optimized business can be missed when a question is interpreted differently from what the marketer intended. Consider these phrases: GEO consultant in Dubai Generative engine optimization consultant in Dubai AI SEO expert in Dubai To a digital marketer, these may appear closely related. But "GEO" is also used in fields such as geology and geotechnical engineering. An AI search system may interpret the abbreviation differently depending on the wording and available context. This was highlighted in an October 2026 visibility test described by Dubai GEO specialist Lopty Pascal, where the abbreviated query produced citations relating to geoscience and engineering rather than generative search optimization. The example illustrates why search visibility testing should use both industry abbreviations and full service names. It also demonstrates the limitations of drawing conclusions from a single prompt. If the intended buyer question is ambiguous, a missing recommendation may say more about the question than about the business itself. For reliable measurement, preserve the precise wording of each question and test relevant variations separately. 6. Do not confuse citations with recommendations This distinction deserves its own measurement system. Imagine asking Perplexity: "What should I consider before hiring a digital marketing consultant in Dubai?" It may cite a useful article from a consultant's website. That does not necessarily mean it is recommending that consultant. Conversely, an assistant might recommend an agency while citing an independent publication discussing the agency's work. For a useful measurement system, track these separately. Metric What it means Brand mention The business appears by name Explicit recommendation The business is presented as an option to choose Website citation A page from the business's website is cited External citation A third-party source about the business is cited Response accuracy The assistant describes the company correctly This is more meaningful than treating every appearance as a ranking win. It also helps distinguish content discovery from provider selection. A technical article might earn citations because it explains a concept well, without generating recommendations for the business that published it. Both outcomes can be useful, but they serve different objectives. 7. Test the same buyer questions repeatedly A single AI response is not a stable measurement of visibility. Answers may vary between platforms, model versions, search configurations, and conversational contexts. Build a small test set based on genuine customer questions. For example, an IT services company could track: Which managed IT service providers operate in Dubai? What cybersecurity consultants serve UAE SMEs? Who can help a growing company with Microsoft 365 migration? Which IT consulting firms specialize in financial services? What should a business check before hiring a managed service provider? Run each question under reasonably consistent conditions. Record the platform, date, complete answer, citations, brand mentions, and recommendations. Separate direct brand-name questions from unprompted category questions. Then observe how the results change over several testing periods. A simple spreadsheet may be sufficient. For businesses operating at scale, dedicated platforms can automate parts of the monitoring process. But API-generated responses and consumer-facing answers should be measured separately, because their configurations and available tools may differ. 8. Fix the specific problem instead of publishing more content blindly One of the easiest mistakes in GEO is assuming every visibility issue can be resolved through additional articles. That is not always the case. A website with inaccessible JavaScript-rendered service pages may need technical changes. A business with inconsistent company descriptions may need to correct its public identity. A company with limited category-specific information may need better service explanations. A business already receiving AI referrals but few conversions may need improved landing pages or a stronger sales process. The right sequence is: Observe the problem → investigate the evidence → identify a plausible cause → implement a targeted change → measure again. This avoids confusing activity with progress. Publishing more content may be helpful when customers genuinely need additional information. But mass-producing similar articles across unrelated websites should not be assumed to improve AI recommendations. Quality, relevance, accessibility, and factual accuracy remain more defensible priorities. What the research actually supports Generative Engine Optimization has attracted academic interest, but it is important to distinguish experiments from guaranteed commercial results. The paper GEO: Generative Engine Optimization , originally published in 2023, introduced a framework for evaluating visibility in generative responses. Its researchers examined techniques involving citations, quotations, statistics, and other content characteristics. Certain methods improved measured visibility under the study's conditions. Those results do not establish that the same techniques will reliably produce identical improvements across today's ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, or Google experiences. Separately, Google's May 2026 guidance on generative AI search reinforces the importance of established SEO practices and genuinely useful content. Taken together, the research and platform documentation support a practical conclusion: AI visibility requires serious technical and information-quality work, but no single optimization method guarantees a brand recommendation. A practical diagnostic checklist Before paying for a large GEO campaign, work through these questions: Can important crawlers access the website's key service pages? Does the initial HTML contain meaningful business information? Does Google index and render the important content correctly? Are the company's name, location, services, and professional identities consistent? Do service pages answer realistic buyer questions? Is the business represented accurately in relevant public sources? Which competing businesses appear in AI-generated recommendations? Are AI responses citing the business, recommending it, or merely mentioning it? Does the company measure these outcomes regularly? Are AI-influenced enquiries being tracked alongside conventional organic search performance? The answers help distinguish technical issues, information gaps, and measurement problems. They also make conversations with SEO agencies and GEO consultants more productive. Final thoughts Ranking well on Google and being recommended by ChatGPT are not equivalent achievements. Traditional rankings measure webpage placement for specific searches. AI recommendation visibility reflects what a generative system says when responding to a particular question. The relationship between the two is important, but it is neither simple nor guaranteed. Google's own guidance confirms that established SEO foundations remain essential for its AI search experiences. Technical specialists working on entity optimization, including Lopty Pascal, highlight additional challenges involving how companies are identified, described, and associated with specific areas of expertise. For businesses, the most useful response is not to abandon SEO or chase every new GEO tactic. It is to investigate accessibility, clarify business identity, improve genuinely useful information, build verifiable evidence, and measure AI-generated responses consistently. A missing recommendation is a signal worth studying, not proof that the entire search strategy has failed. title: Confirming cash-on-delivery orders on WhatsApp without the API, in the browser
author: Low Key Builds
summary: Most online orders in Pakistan are cash on delivery. Sellers who run ads get a steady stream of fake or careless orders, and every refused parcel costs two-way courier charges. So most small stores do one manual step before booking the courier: they message each customer on WhatsApp and ask them to confirm. The paid fix is a Shopify app on the WhatsApp Business API (there are several, from about $3 to $10 a month plus Meta's per-message fees). I wanted to see how far a free, static, browser-only tool could go for the sellers who do not have Shopify or do not want the API: WooCommerce stores, and Instagram and Facebook sellers who keep orders in a Google Sheet. The result is ConfirmKaro , which I built. Here is what was interesting to build. 1. wa.me links do the sending WhatsApp has a public click-to-chat URL: https://wa.me/<number>?text=<urlencoded message> . On a phone it opens the chat in the WhatsApp app with the message typed; on desktop it opens WhatsApp Web. The seller presses send. No API, no number registration, no template approval, and the message comes from the shop's normal WhatsApp, which customers already recognise. The cost is one tap per order, which is fine up to a few dozen orders a day. 2. Pakistani phone numbers in the wild wa.me wants the international format with no + , no spaces and no leading zero: 923001234567 . Order exports contain everything else: 0300 1234567 -> 923001234567 +92 321 7654321 -> 923217654321 0333-5556667 -> 923335556667 3001234567 -> 923001234567 (leading zero lost by Excel) 00923001234567 -> 923001234567 03451234 -> invalid (too short) function normPhone ( raw ) { const s = String ( raw || '' ). trim (); const plus = s . startsWith ( ' + ' ); let d = s . replace ( / \D /g , '' ); if ( d . startsWith ( ' 0092 ' )) d = d . slice ( 2 ); if ( d . length === 11 && d . startsWith ( ' 03 ' )) d = ' 92 ' + d . slice ( 1 ); else if ( d . length === 10 && d . startsWith ( ' 3 ' )) d = ' 92 ' + d ; if ( d . length === 12 && d . startsWith ( ' 923 ' )) return { ok : true , wa : d , pk : true }; if ( plus && d . length >= 10 && d . length <= 15 ) return { ok : true , wa : d , pk : false }; return { ok : false , wa : d }; } The Excel case matters more than it looks: when a sheet stores the number as a number, the leading zero disappears, so a 10-digit value starting with 3 is almost certainly a Pakistani mobile. 3. Shopify exports one row per line item Shopify's orders CSV repeats the order Name ( #1041 ) on one row per item, and only the first row has the total and shipping details. Merging by order number and appending item rows gives one message per order. WooCommerce export plugins use different headers ( Billing Phone , Order Total Amount ), so columns are matched by a ranked list of header tests, and the user can override any column. 4. Fake-order flags without any server All local heuristics: invalid number, the same number on several orders in the batch, an address under 12 characters ("abc"), a name with digits or fewer than three letters, and a total over four times the batch median. None of these prove fraud; they decide who gets confirmed most carefully. 5. Urdu in Nastaliq, and Roman Urdu Most sellers write to customers in Roman Urdu ("Order confirm karne ke liye 1 likh kar bhejein"), some in Urdu script, some in English. The templates come in all three. The page self-hosts Noto Nastaliq Urdu (SIL OFL) as a 160 KB woff2 converted with fontTools, sets lang="ur" dir="rtl" , and needs a line height above 2 because Nastaliq stacks vertically. WhatsApp renders the Urdu text itself with the phone's font, so the font only matters on the page. 6. Nothing leaves the browser The CSV is read with FileReader , statuses (pending, confirmed, no reply, cancelled) live in localStorage , and the confirmed orders download as a CSV for courier bulk booking. Customer names and phone numbers never touch a server, which is the main reason a seller can trust a tool from someone they do not know. What I would like to know If you build stores for Pakistani (or Indian, Bangladeshi, Egyptian, Moroccan) COD sellers: how do your clients confirm orders today, and what format does their courier's bulk booking want? Replies at confirmkaro@appin60.com or in the comments shape what gets added next. Disclosure: I built ConfirmKaro. It is free and has no paid tier.

title: Building a Browser-Based Image Tool: Lessons from CompressFly
author: Ethan Carter
summary: What batch processing, memory limits, lazy loading, and downloads taught me about frontend development. An image compressor looks like a small frontend project: select a file, adjust the quality, press a button, and save the result. Add a folder of high-resolution photos, a phone with limited memory, and a download that needs to contain every successful result, and the engineering problem gets more interesting. I’m building CompressFly , a browser-based toolkit for everyday file tasks. Its image compression and conversion tools process images locally in the browser. Working on those tools has made me think more carefully about what happens between selecting a file and actually finishing the job. The useful lessons reach beyond image tools. They apply to document editors, media utilities, import screens, and other web applications that do substantial work on a user’s device. 1. Local processing changes where the constraints live For image compression and format conversion, keeping the work in the browser means the source images do not need to be uploaded to a processing server. That is useful, but it also makes the user’s device part of the processing environment. Available memory, other open tabs, and the size of the selected images all affect what the application can comfortably handle. The website still needs to load its application resources. Local image processing is a statement about where the image work happens; it is not a promise that the entire site works offline. That distinction belongs in the interface. Someone deciding whether to select personal photos should be able to understand the data flow without knowing how the application is built. My takeaway: explain the boundary of a privacy claim as carefully as the benefit. A specific explanation is more useful than a broad “everything is secure” badge. 2. File size is a poor estimate of working memory A photo that occupies a few megabytes on disk can require much more memory once decoded. For a simple example, consider a 6,000 × 4,000 image represented as four 8-bit color channels. That pixel buffer alone contains: * 6,000 × 4,000 × 4 = 96,000,000 bytes, or about 92 MiB. * This is an illustrative calculation, not a measurement of CompressFly. It excludes the original file, output data, previews, and any temporary allocations. MDN’s ImageData documentation describes the underlying pixel representation, including RGBA channel order. That helps explain why “the total upload size looks small” is not enough to judge a batch. It also changes the questions worth asking during development. How many images need to be decoded at once? Does a small preview need the full-resolution source? How long does temporary data remain reachable after an operation ends? Those questions matter even when the interface looks simple. A sensible memory budget can determine whether a tool remains usable on the device someone already has. 3. A batch needs scheduling, not just a loop Suppose someone selects 40 product photos. Starting all 40 operations immediately may look efficient, but it can also create a burst of decoding, temporary buffers, and result updates. A more useful way to think about the problem is a queue with a bounded amount of active work. When one task finishes, another can start. One slow image should not prevent unrelated work from continuing. There is no universally correct concurrency setting. Image dimensions, processing cost, and device resources all matter. A processor count alone does not tell you how much image data a browser can safely keep in memory. The interface also needs to distinguish files waiting for their turn from files actively being processed. Otherwise, a perfectly ordinary queue can look like a stalled application. Batch processing changes the meaning of success, too. If one image fails, users still need to know which other images completed and what they can save. A single error message for the entire folder hides information they need to finish the task. That is why I think of batch support as a workflow feature. Accepting multiple files is only the beginning. 4. Lazy loading needs a plan for the first click A file tool can accumulate dependencies for previews, encoders, archives, and downloads. Loading every optional feature at the start makes a visitor pay for work they may never use. JavaScript’s dynamic import provides a way to load modules asynchronously when needed. The product question is when that need becomes likely. For a preview or download feature, an early interaction can be a useful hint. Pointer interaction and keyboard focus matter alongside desktop hover; a phone user should have an equally reliable path. Preloading remains an optimization. The actual action must still wait for the required feature to be ready and handle a loading failure. Several interactions should share the same loading work rather than create competing initialization paths. A failed background load also needs a deliberate retry policy. Otherwise, an optimization can quietly leave a feature unusable for the rest of the session. This is the part of lazy loading I find easy to underestimate: splitting the bundle is only one piece of making a deferred feature feel dependable. 5. Stopping work and ignoring old results are separate problems Asynchronous work can outlive the interface that started it. Imagine a user begins processing, stops, and starts again with different settings. An earlier operation may finish after the new one has begun. If its result is still accepted, the screen can show an output that belongs to the previous request. The same issue appears in search suggestions and image editors. The operation completed successfully, but its result is no longer relevant. Cancellation helps, provided the underlying work cooperates with the signal. The browser’s AbortController API supports signaling cancellation; it does not automatically make arbitrary computation stop. The application also needs a clear rule for whether a result still belongs to the current task. That rule matters for errors and cleanup as well as successful results. An old failure should not overwrite a newer success message. Thinking through these cases early makes the interface easier to reason about. A button labeled “Stop” creates an expectation about everything that happens afterward. 6. The download is part of the processing workflow Converting 40 images and requiring 40 separate downloads leaves a large part of the original repetitive task in place. For supported batch workflows, collecting completed files in a ZIP makes the output easier to save together. But archiving introduces its own decisions: which results belong in the archive, how filenames are handled, and what happens if the preferred download method is unavailable. There is also a distinction between packaging and compression. A ZIP is useful for grouping images, but already-compressed image files may not become much smaller inside it. Memory matters again at this stage. Building an entire archive in memory and writing output progressively have different resource requirements. Browser support and failure handling need to be considered along with the preferred path. Progressive output also does not eliminate memory already occupied by retained results. The CompressFly image compressor brings these concerns into one visible workflow: select images, choose settings, review the results, and download completed files individually or together. That final step deserves the same attention as the processing button. Users came for files they can use elsewhere. What I would focus on when building another file tool I would start with a complete, modest workflow: one file, an understandable result, and a working download. Then I would introduce mixed batches, delayed dependencies, failures, and repeated actions. The questions I would keep nearby are practical: Can the user tell what is waiting, working, finished, or failed? Is the amount of active work appropriate for the available resources? Can an old operation change a newer result? Does a deferred feature still work when preloading never happened? Can the user recover completed files when part of a batch fails? Building a browser-based image tool has given me a better appreciation for these ordinary details. The visible operation may be “compress this image,” but the development work stretches from the first file selection to the last saved result. I’m continuing that work in CompressFly. For a concrete example, you can try its HEIC to JPG converter and follow the path from a batch of source photos to downloadable copies.

title: Supabase vs Firebase in 2026: SQL Freedom or Real-Time Maturity?
author: TechLogHub
summary: Supabase and Firebase both promise "a backend without running a backend". They get there in very different ways, and picking the wrong one is expensive to undo. The 30-second version: The real difference: the data model Supabase runs on Postgres , a relational SQL database. If your data has clear relationships (users, orders, line items), you get joins, constraints and SQL you already know. Firebase uses Firestore , a NoSQL document database. It suits flexible, denormalised structures and shines when the shape of your data changes often. Real-time and mobile This is Firebase's home turf. Real-time sync is one of its original core strengths and is highly mature, and its native iOS and Android SDKs are deep. Supabase's real-time is functional but less established. If you're building a mobile-first app that lives on live data, Firebase still has the edge. Lock-in and exit paths Supabase is open source and can be self-hosted, so you have a way out if pricing or policy changes. Firebase is fully proprietary with no comparable exit option. One practical gotcha: Supabase free-tier projects pause after 7 days of inactivity, so keep that in mind for side projects and demos. So which one? Relational data, web-first or full-stack app, want an open-source exit path: Supabase. Native mobile app, deep SDK integration, mature real-time sync, fine with NoSQL and lock-in: Firebase.
